title: Boss: controllers in code
summary: Three workload tickets on a real Kubernetes cluster: set-based selection, a failed CronJob, and a DaemonSet that runs nowhere.

steps.title: The scene
body: Workload tickets, each on its own one-node **Kubernetes 1.37** cluster: a clean-up that must hit exactly the right
pods, a nightly job that failed, and an agent that should run on every node but runs on none. Use selectors,
`kubectl create job --from=cronjob/...`, `kubectl logs`, `kubectl describe` and `kubectl taint`/`label`.

steps.title: Ticket 1: select exactly the right pods
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). The same ten labelled pods as in the labels lesson run in `default`.
1. Write into `~/answers/api.txt` the pods with `tier=api` in `prod` **or** `staging` that are **not** canaries (they
2. Pods without an `env` label are strays. **Delete** them, and only them, with one label selector.

checks.name: the strays are gone, nothing else
checks.cmd: kubectl get pods -o name | cut -d/ -f2 | sort | xargs
checks.expectOutput: cart-1 cart-2 cart-3 pay-1 pay-2 pay-3 report-1 search-1 search-2
checks.fail: Only `debug-1` has no `env` label. `kubectl delete pods -l '!env'`.

hints: Set-based selectors: `key in (a,b)`, `key notin (a)`, `key` (exists) and `!key` (does not exist).
Always look before you delete: `kubectl get pods -l '!env'` shows what the same selector would delete.
`kubectl get pods -l 'tier=api,env in (prod,staging),!canary' -o name`, then `kubectl delete pods -l '!env'`.
solution: kubectl get pods -l 'tier=api,env in (prod,staging),!canary' -o name | cut -d/ -f2 > ~/answers/api.txt
steps.explain: These are the same `matchExpressions` operators (`In`, `NotIn`, `Exists`, `DoesNotExist`) that Deployments, NetworkPolicies and affinity rules use in YAML. Running the selector with `get` before `delete` is the habit that prevents deleting a whole namespace's pods with a typo.

steps.title: Ticket 2: the nightly export failed
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). The CronJob `nightly-export` runs at 02:30 UTC. Last night's run (re-run by hand as the Job
`nightly-export-manual-1`) failed. Find out why from its pod's log, fix the **CronJob** (not just one Job: the
container's command is right, the configuration it reads is not), and prove the fix by running the CronJob's job
**now**, by hand, as a Job named `nightly-export-manual-2`, which must complete.

checks.name: nightly-export-manual-2 completed
checks.fail: `nightly-export-manual-2` has not completed. `kubectl create job nightly-export-manual-2 --from=cronjob/nightly-export`, then `kubectl wait --for=condition=Complete job/...`.

checks.name: its log shows the export
checks.fail: The job did not export to the target.

checks.name: the CronJob itself is fixed
checks.cmd: kubectl get cronjob nightly-export -o json | jq -r '.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec.containers[0].command[-1]' | grep -c TARGET_URL
checks.fail: Keep the container's command as it is; fix the configuration it reads.

hints: `kubectl logs job/nightly-export-manual-1` shows the error; `kubectl get configmap export-config -o yaml` shows what the job gets.
The ConfigMap's key is `TARGET`, the command reads `TARGET_URL`: rename the key, or set `TARGET_URL` in the CronJob's container env.

`kubectl create configmap export-config --from-literal=TARGET_URL=s3://reports.example.com/nightly --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -`, then `kubectl create job nightly-export-manual-2 --from=cronjob/nightly-export` and `kubectl wait --for=condition=Complete job/nightly-export-manual-2`.
solution: kubectl create configmap export-config --from-literal=TARGET_URL=s3://reports.example.com/nightly --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
steps.explain: `kubectl create job --from=cronjob/X` runs a CronJob's exact template now, which is how you test a fix without waiting until 02:30. `--dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -` is the idiom for "create or update this generated object". Remember that `envFrom` reads the ConfigMap when the pod starts: running pods never see a change, new ones do.

steps.title: Ticket 3: the log agent runs nowhere
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). The DaemonSet `log-agent` in `kube-system` should run one pod on every logging node, but
`kubectl get ds -n kube-system log-agent` shows `DESIRED 0`. The node `dojo` **is** a logging node, and it is
reserved for observability workloads with a taint.
Without removing the taint, make `log-agent` run its pod on `dojo`: label the node the way the DaemonSet expects, and
let the DaemonSet tolerate the taint.

checks.name: log-agent runs on dojo
checks.fail: `log-agent` should have 1 desired and 1 ready pod.

checks.name: the taint is still there
checks.fail: Keep the node's `dedicated=observability:NoSchedule` taint: tolerate it instead.

checks.name: the node is labelled as a logging node
checks.fail: Label the node with what the DaemonSet's `nodeSelector` asks for.

hints: `kubectl get ds log-agent -n kube-system -o yaml` shows its `nodeSelector`; `kubectl describe node dojo` shows labels and taints.
Add `tolerations: [{key: dedicated, operator: Equal, value: observability, effect: NoSchedule}]` to the pod template, for example with `kubectl patch ds log-agent -n kube-system -p '...'`.
solution: kubectl -n kube-system get ds log-agent -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.nodeSelector}'; echo
kubectl describe node dojo | grep -A2 -i taints
steps.explain: A DaemonSet puts one pod on each node that its `nodeSelector` (or affinity) matches **and** whose taints it tolerates. Taints repel, tolerations allow: they keep general workloads off dedicated nodes while letting the right agents in. Real clusters' log, metrics and CNI agents all carry broad tolerations for exactly this reason.
